    <title>Realized versus Population Reliability: Anytime-Valid Self-Consistency Certification under Correlated Reasoning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:47:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26592v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26592v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Self-consistency certification treats repeated sampling from a language model as sequential evidence accumulation and stops when an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold, guaranteeing finite-sample Type I error control by Ville's inequality. Prior constructions assume sampled rollouts are conditionally independent. We show this assumption fails in practice: reasoning streams are positively correlated through shared reasoning prefixes or across-prompt heterogeneity, changing not merely certificate efficiency but the hypothesis certified. Modeling dependence via a per-unit latent state (the random-effects / intraclass-correlation structure) induces exchangeable, equi-correlated increments with correlation $ρ$. Correlation splits the single null into a realized null about the drawn belief and a population null about average model behavior, which coincide only when $ρ=0$. We show: (i) the standard betting e-process remains anytime-valid for the realized null, not the population null; (ii) read as a population-null test, a suitable mixture has asymptotic crossing probability at least $π=P(μ(Z)>0)$, potentially exceeding nominal $ε$; (iii) the within-unit mean's effective sample size saturates at $1/ρ$, so extra within-unit rollouts cannot restore population validity; and (iv) a prompt-level e-process restores population validity, with optimal allocation at one rollout per prompt under a pure rollout budget. Simulations and Claude Haiku 4.5 rollouts confirm this regime dependence: on GSM8K ($\hatρ=0.435$, $\hatθ=+0.96$) the gap is dormant, whereas on AIME ($\hatρ=0.480$, $\hatθ=-0.15$) the single-unit rule crosses on 24% of prompts at nominal $ε=0.05$, while the prompt-level procedure declines (0.00). This correctness result identifies which reliability claim an anytime-valid certificate actually supports under dependence.</summary>

    <title>Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:46:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26590v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26590v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.</summary>

    <summary>A passing UVM regression shows the design agrees with the reference model on what the scoreboard checks, not that it meets the specification.     <title>High-Accuracy Neural-Network Quantum States via Randomized Real-Time Dynamics</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:45:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26587v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26587v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Neural-network quantum states (NQSs) exhibit a disparity in converging to the ground state during energy minimization: while the energy converges quadratically with the error in the variational wave function, other observables converge only linearly, which limits the accuracy of physical predictions. Here we show how to close this gap by introducing a new algorithm that improves the accuracy of NQSs. Our method, termed dynamical averaging, estimates expectation values by averaging over a state (or observable) evolved in real-time. Using insights from quantum information, we prove an up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground state observables, thus matching the fast convergence of the energy. Importantly, this improved accuracy requires neither further energy minimization nor increased model complexity, but rather exploits the effect of randomization on quantum states. We demonstrate dynamical averaging on non-integrable spin models, where it accelerates convergence and substantially reduces errors in observables.</summary>

    <title>ProtoDiffusion: Token-per-Layer Generative Modeling of Multi-Layer Images</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:45:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26586v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26586v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse. Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representation size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the layers. We present ProtoDiffusion, a latent-diffusion framework built on ProtoVAE, a multi-layer variational autoencoder that encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and one candidate vector per layer. Each candidate conditions a shared decoder to reconstruct its corresponding RGBA layer. For $N$ layers, the representation contains $HW+N$ tokens before backbone-specific packing, compared with $NHW$ for full-grid-per-layer representations. ProtoDiffusion jointly denoises the prototype and a fixed set of candidate slots, conditioned on an image or text, with bounding boxes as optional layout guidance. The model leaves unneeded slots empty and determines the number of layers and, in absence of boxes, their layout, requiring neither as input. The same architecture supports both image-to-design and text-to-design. ProtoVAE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction from its compact shared latent representation, reaching 40.43 dB PSNR on layer crops. On the LayerD evaluation split, image-to-design achieves RGB L1 scores of 0.040 with bounding boxes and 0.057 without, with box-guided alpha soft IoU (0.850) comparable to the strongest fine-tuned baseline (0.871). On merged images, text-to-design reaches 66.41 FID versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein], achieves a 0.860 text-accuracy score, and runs $19.1\times$ faster than the same-backbone generation-then-decomposition cascade.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26584v1</id>
    <title>Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:43:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26584v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26584v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($Δd' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26582v1</id>
    <title>End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:43:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26582v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26582v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points $N_g$ and the inverse of the desired accuracy $\varepsilon$, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in $N_g$ and quasilinear in $1/\varepsilon$. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in $N_g$ and $1/\varepsilon$. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with $N_g$ over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26577v1</id>
    <title>Classically Trained Quantum Generative Models with Shared Training and Fine Tuning for Quantum Matter</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:42:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26577v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26577v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Ground-state measurement statistics characterize quantum matter. Selected correlations can guide the classical training of a quantum sampler even when sampling the full distribution is difficult. We ask whether training across related ground-state distributions helps the sampler reproduce their correlations more accurately. We train a hypernetwork to map Hamiltonian parameters to circuit angles, sharing information across the phase diagram before local fine-tuning with additional reference data for quantum deployment. For classical training, we derive an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of Fourier coefficients for circuits built from general Pauli rotations, with a cost that depends on the circuit generators. We also introduce a CDF-KL loss for comparing selected marginals. We study the Haldane Hamiltonian and transverse-field Ising model, using an automated search to select reference calculations near phase transitions. On the twelve-site chain, the adaptively pretrained hypernetwork matches the independent fits' final mean total variation distance in fewer local updates and continues to a lower error. On a 1,024-site chain and a 4 by 256 lattice, the fine-tuned circuits have lower squared maximum mean discrepancy from the reference distributions than the independent circuits at the evaluated point in each geometry. These results motivate shared training for preparing quantum samplers across a phase diagram and local fine-tuning.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26574v1</id>
    <title>Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:40:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26574v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26574v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026.
  Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$.
  Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof.
  Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).</summary>

    <title>Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs</title>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26569v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.</summary>

    <summary>Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.</summary>

    <title>Multi-institutional grading of Barrett's esophagus dysplasia without stain normalization using a pathology foundation model and multiple instance learning</title>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26562v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26562v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Barrett's esophagus dysplasia grading suffers substantial inter-observer variability, particularly for low-grade dysplasia, complicating clinical decision-making. We conducted a retrospective multi-institutional diagnostic accuracy study of a foundation model-based deep learning system for dysplasia grading, using 969 H\&E-stained whole slide images from four institutions. Patch-level classifiers trained on expert annotations identified diagnostically relevant regions, followed by attribute-aware multiple instance learning for slide-level classification as non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus (NDBE), low-grade dysplasia, or high-grade dysplasia. On a held-out test set (n = 130), macro-averaged AUC was 0.96 (95\% CI 0.93--0.98). For binary dysplasia detection, sensitivity was 98\% (80/82) and specificity 81\% (39/48), with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.030 and quadratic-weighted \kap{} of 0.83 against expert consensus. No high-grade dysplasia case was misclassified as NDBE. Performance was consistent across institutions without stain normalization, indicating that stain-robust foundation-model representations may remove the site-specific preprocessing that has constrained prior systems to institution-specific deployment.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26557v1</id>
    <title>MM-SystemOneBias: Evaluating Bias in Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:25:41Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26557v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26557v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>When multimodal decision models determine actions, moderation outcomes, or quality judgments, their reliability depends on preserving semantic decisions across presentation changes, ignoring irrelevant additions, and distinguishing information consistent with task evidence from information that conflicts with it. Existing evaluations study decision-interface biases and multimodal model behavior in separate settings, leaving no common protocol to compare multimodal decision models with their backbones on practical tasks. We introduce \textbf{MM-SystemOneBias}, which evaluates 13 models on 5,323 original instances from nine public datasets and 11 task scenarios using six paired interventions: option order, option label, external judgment, image--text description, irrelevant information, and rating scale. Across seven matched decision-model--backbone pairs, decision models are more stable under option-label, irrelevant-information, and rating-scale changes in all seven pairs; six pairs also show lower option-order flip rates. They incur smaller accuracy losses under incorrect external judgments in all seven pairs and conflicting descriptions in six. In six pairs, they gain less accuracy from correct external judgments and show less favorable accuracy changes under consistent descriptions. Among pairs with unchanged semantic decisions, mean absolute changes in answer probabilities range from 4.56 to 11.55 percentage points, revealing input effects that accuracy alone misses.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26553v1</id>
    <title>Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:23:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26553v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26553v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.</summary>

    <title>The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:20:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26545v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26545v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Linear probes are the cheapest LLM lie detectors but often fail to transfer across kinds of lie. Label-free directions from honest and deceptive role-play are untested at 70B scale and on lies about knowledge, where a lie and an honest denial can be identical. We widen a published persona bank with roles that deny knowledge they have, plus honest counterparts. At each model's middle layer the resulting persona direction ranks lies across Liars' Bench better than single-dataset probes on three of its four models; it fails on Qwen, even when Qwen stays in role far more often. On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct it beats directions from a random persona bank, but its gain over the published direction is within the range of random widenings. On lies about knowledge, persona directions mainly track a reply's wording: where lies and honest denials share their words, our three main contrasts stay inside the random-direction band on Llama and Qwen and reach only its edge on Gemma, though on Mistral one clears it. A knowledge direction contrasts questions the model can answer with ones nobody can, each followed by the same scripted denial. It separates lies from identical honest denials on two models and narrowly on a third, but not on the fourth; its other results partly depend on the benchmark's wording. On the Gender-Secret fine-tune it clears the band by a few hundredths on Llama and fails on Mistral. The sum of the two directions ranks lies better than a supervised probe at the same depth on all four models (on one, both near chance) but is level with the persona direction on Llama's average and behind that probe on held-out lies. More varied role-play questions do not help the persona direction on Liars' Bench.</summary>

    <title>Authenticating quantum key distribution through random position checks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:18:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26542v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26542v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum key distribution (QKD) requires some form of authentication in order for the parties to be sure they are not unknowingly generating a key with an adversary pretending to be one of the honest parties. In this work, we propose a protocol in which the position of one of the parties is used as the authentication credential for key distribution. Our protocol essentially consists of a BB84 QKD protocol with quantum position verification (QPV) rounds randomly interleaved in. The approach is efficient compared with previous approaches, which required running an entire QPV protocol for every bit requiring authentication. We undertake an initial security analysis of the protocol for a restricted set of attacks.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26540v1</id>
    <title>AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:17:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26540v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26540v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26538v1</id>
    <title>LLM GerryMandering: Separating Interactions from Additive Effects in LLM Audits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:16:40Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26538v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26538v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Intersectional bias arises when a model treats people who hold several marginalised identities at once differently from what their separate identities would predict. Auditing such intersectional subgroups remains a challenge: their number grows quadratically, and there is no agreed baseline for what independent attributes would predict. Without such a baseline, many existing audits flag a subgroup when it exceeds each attribute alone, a condition that attributes acting independently already satisfy. We test this standard criterion on 150 synthetic datasets built with no interaction. With the shuffle null, it flags 66.1 false subgroups per dataset on average, and at least one in every dataset. When we plant interactions of known size into these datasets, a repaired null lets the criterion recover only 32% of them. We introduce ADDIS (Additive Intersectional Screen), which fits an additive model over all attributes, scores each subgroup by its Additive Residual Distance (ARD) from that model's prediction, and tests it against a Freedman-Lane null. On our synthetic benchmark, ADDIS flags 0.09 false subgroups per dataset and recovers 84% of the same planted interactions. We then build IndiPersona, 10,000 synthetic Indian personas with six identity attributes, and audit 13 open language models. The standard criterion flags 7.1% of the 738 tested subgroups on average; ADDIS flags 3.0%. Gender identity crossed with sexual orientation is the largest pairing in every model, and counterfactual personas confirm it and additionally reveal a caste x class interaction in all but one model that the observational test lacked the data to detect. Much of what audits report as intersectional bias can thus arise from independent single-attribute effects alone, yet a small core of interactions survives.</summary>

    <title>On the design of sequential quantum repeaters with error detection</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:16:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26537v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26537v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Long-distance, trust-free quantum communications rely on the development of scalable quantum repeater schemes. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is a promising approach that combines manageable implementation requirements with a hop-by-hop architecture compatible with existing classical infrastructure. In this paper, we investigate key design choices for such schemes over a repeater chain using quantum key distribution as a benchmark. We find that simple quantum error-detecting codes, such as repetition codes or quantum parity codes, perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform strategies without any encoding. In particular, we show that two-qubit repetition codes may well be all that we need to implement in many practical scenarios. We also examine different architectures for the generation of initial entanglement and assess their merits. Additionally, we show that moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially mitigate the slow technological progress of others.</summary>

    <title>Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:12:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26531v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26531v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. In this system, LLM agents propose hypotheses, and deterministic tools execute experiments and verify them. For each model, an LLM generates and shortlists cross features from a combinatorial candidate space, and all features are then ranked by several importance methods. Feature blending mixes these rankings into a single selection, using Pareto fronts across tasks for multi-task models. An LLM Researcher agent then tunes the feature selection in 10--25 asynchronous trials under resource caps, and a trimming step keeps the pipeline cost within budget. Across production models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31% on average within each model's budget, and the trimming step cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% with no regression beyond measurement noise. The optimized models were launched, and in online A/B tests they improved a primary online metric by 0.20%.</summary>

    <title>Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:01:28Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26525v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26525v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.</summary>

    <title>Hamiltonian Stabilization of the Two-Photon Dicke Model</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:00:36Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26523v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26523v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Collective two-photon light--matter interactions enable pair amplification but can destroy spectral confinement, preventing a stable thermodynamic bright phase. We show that a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr interaction renders the two-photon Dicke Hamiltonian of \(N\) emitters lower-bounded at all couplings while preserving its generalized \(\mathbb Z_4\) symmetry. We determine the exact zero-temperature thermodynamic energy density with \(O(N^{-1})\) finite-size control and obtain the global phase diagram. A bright minimum is born at a saddle-node and exchanges global stability with the normal minimum at coexistence, producing a discontinuous photon-density jump. Symmetry-resolved exact diagonalization through \(N=128\) supports the predicted density jump and an exponentially closing same-sector normal--bright tunneling gap. Spectral collapse thus becomes the singular zero-Kerr point of a first-order phase diagram, identifying a Hamiltonian route to stabilizing pair amplification.</summary>

    <summary>Reliable extraction of calcium-dependent fluorescence traces in calcium imaging sequences requires identifying pixels whose fluorescence intensity reflects the same underlying cellular activity. We present a deterministic temporal embedding framework that maps pixel-wise fluorescence traces to a low-dimensional representation in which temporally coherent sources form spatially coherent regions. Starting from a fuzzy-neighborhood graph and spectral initialization, we optimize a class-balanced cross-entropy objective using exact sparse attraction and a deterministic particle-mesh decomposition of the dense repulsive interaction with sparse edge compensation, avoiding stochastic negative sampling. The resulting latent representation is spatially decoded into reliable source supports for trace extraction without imposing an explicit cellular shape prior. Experiments on synthetic and in vivo two-photon calcium imaging data demonstrate robust recovery of irregular and spatially touching sources together with efficient deterministic embedding optimization.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26521v1</id>
    <title>The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity, and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:00:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26521v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26521v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In our experiments on long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, a longer observation window outweighed the observed effects of more data, more capacity and newer architectures. The window is the weeks of history a model sees before the week it forecasts from. Going from an 8- to a 16-week window adds a raw +0.070 to 0.107 log-space $R^2$ in every family at 1M. Matched test cohorts, which score the same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets, four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal data, longer windows admit up to 10% more and colder training customers, which matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in one eight-week band. On training-period anchors, the weekly ridge probe's gain persists outside the holiday season, keeping about 72% of it. We therefore report a robust positive association with longer windows and do not identify the magnitude of a calendar-independent history effect. Of four internally registered predictions, the only fully blind one failed. An activity-mixture model predicted +0.014 from 24 to 32 weeks; the weekly-aggregate probe returned -0.0004. For the sequence families, the other three levers are about an order of magnitude smaller, bounded and unresolved. Their observed effects are at most 0.006 between the nominal 1M and 10M tiers and 0.0052 among five sequence families at 16 weeks with clocks as built, both single-seed on the full test split, and 0.006 for capacity on three-seed means. These are observed intervals, not equivalence bounds. Our claim is the order-of-magnitude contrast between the window and those bounds. A team building on this class of data should start by lengthening the window.</summary>

    <title>Simple Private Noisy SGD is Minimax-Optimal under Population Strong Convexity</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T17:58:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26515v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26515v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is at the center of modern machine learning and is known to be statistically minimax-optimal in many regression settings, e.g., for convex Generalized Linear Models (GLMs). Yet, it is unknown whether its simplest differentially private Noisy SGD counterpart fulfills similar favorable guarantees even on strongly convex losses. We resolve this question affirmatively. We upper bound the parameter estimation error for a single pass of Noisy SGD with a fixed stepsize schedule and constant batch sizes on smooth and strongly convex Lipschitz losses over a compact convex domain under Renyi DP. Specialized to strongly convex GLMs, our error bounds match minimax lower bounds we derive based on the Score Attack framework. In particular, this provides the first minimax-optimal rate for Noisy SGD in private logistic regression, avoiding poly-logarithmic terms present in existing results. Our analysis is versatile as it relies on standard convex analysis and establishes the same rates in expectation and with high probability.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26514v1</id>
    <title>Hybrid Retrieval for Government Scheme Search in English and Marathi</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T17:58:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26514v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26514v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Retrieving government schemes requires matching citizens' information needs to formal administrative descriptions, often across languages and terminology. We present a bilingual search system for Maharashtra government schemes and public services that combines BM25 retrieval with sentence-embedding similarity through equal-weight score fusion. The system indexes aligned English-Marathi scheme descriptions and supports multilingual, Marathi-focused, and translation-mediated semantic configurations. Evaluation on manually curated bilingual queries compares BM25, dense retrieval, and hybrid retrieval using IndicSBERT and MahaSBERT. BM25 provides a strong baseline with a mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.864. Hybrid retrieval increases MRR to 0.872 with IndicSBERT and 0.879 with MahaSBERT, whereas the corresponding dense-only systems achieve 0.663 and 0.655. MahaSBERT-based fusion also increases precision from 0.781 to 0.808 while matching BM25 recall at 0.946. These results support the complementary use of lexical and semantic signals in this collection, while showing that improvements over a strong lexical baseline are modest and metric-dependent. The study provides an application-focused analysis of hybrid retrieval for bilingual public-service information access.</summary>

{"protocolSection":{"identificationModule":{"nctId":"NCT00230035","orgStudyIdInfo":{"id":"DAIT SCSLE-01"},"organization":{"fullName":"National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)","class":"NIH"},"briefTitle":"Lupus Immunosuppressive/Immunomodulatory Therapy or Stem Cell Transplant (LIST)","officialTitle":"A Randomized, Open Label, Phase II Multicenter Study of Non-Myeloablative Autologous Transplantation With Auto-CD34+HPC Versus Currently Available Immunosuppressive/Immunomodulatory Therapy for Treatment of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus"},"statusModule":{"statusVerifiedDate":"2013-01","overallStatus":"WITHDRAWN","whyStopped":"Recommended by DSMB due to lack of accrual","expandedAccessInfo":{"hasExpandedAccess":false},"startDateStruct":{"date":"2005-09"},"studyFirstSubmitDate":"2005-09-28","studyFirstSubmitQcDate":"2005-09-28","studyFirstPostDateStruct":{"date":"2005-09-30","type":"ESTIMATED"},"lastUpdateSubmitDate":"2013-01-31","lastUpdatePostDateStruct":{"date":"2013-02-01","type":"ESTIMATED"}},"sponsorCollaboratorsModule":{"responsibleParty":{"type":"SPONSOR"},"leadSponsor":{"name":"National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)","class":"NIH"}},"oversightModule":{"oversightHasDmc":true},"descriptionModule":{"briefSummary":"Systemic lupus erythematosus, also known as lupus or SLE, is a chronic, multisystem, autoimmune disease in which the body's internal system of defense attacks its own normal tissues. This abnormal autoimmune response can result in damage to many parts of the body, especially the skin, joints, lungs, heart, brain, intestines, and kidneys. Both genetic and environmental risk factors are involved in the development of lupus, but these are poorly understood.

SLE has an overall 10-year survival between 80 and 90%. However, we estimate that severe lupus not responding to the usual available treatments has a 50% mortality rate in 10 years. Kidney problems occur in 30% to 50% of lupus patients and may progress to kidney failure. Kidney disease due to lupus occurs more frequently in African-Americans and Hispanics. Lupus can affect many parts of the body and cause damage, but the severe form can result in death from kidney disease; cardiovascular disease, specifically atherosclerosis; central nervous system disease; and infections.

Currently, no single standard therapy for treatment of severe SLE exists. Usually physicians prescribe an aggressive regimen of one or a combination of immunosuppressive/immunomodulatory treatments. This approach to therapy for all forms of severe SLE derives largely from studies of lupus nephritis. Current treatment, although effective in many people, are not effective in all patients and are associated with drug-induced morbidity. The design of the control arm for this study reflects the current status of treatment of SLE in the academic setting. Investigators may choose from a list of commonly used and currently available immunosuppressive/immunomodulatory treatments to optimize the treatment of their patients, based on their past treatment history and response to those treatments. Study treatments may consist of corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide (CTX), azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), rituximab, and leflunomide. Treatment may be changed as frequently and as necessary within the first year of the study to control the manifestations of SLE in each patient. New therapies that become available during the course of this trial may be added to the list of approved medications for this study.

In response to the absence of a uniformly effective treatment for severe lupus, autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has been proposed as a potential therapy. Hematopoietic stem cells are immature blood cells that can develop into all of the different blood and immune cells the body uses. Researchers believe that resetting the immune system may stop or slow down the progression of the disease. The main purpose of this study is to compare two ways of treating SLE: 1) high-dose immunosuppressive therapy (HDIT) followed by HSCT and 2) currently available immunosuppressive/immunomodulatory therapies.","detailedDescription":"SLE is a chronic, multisystem, inflammatory autoimmune disease in which the body's immune cells wrongly attack its own tissues. It is defined by the presence of circulating antinuclear antibodies that are directed against nucleosomal DNA-histone complexes, native double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (Sm and RNP), single-stranded DNA, and phospholipids moieties on platelets and other tissues, indicating a failure of the regulatory systems involved in maintenance of immunologic tolerance to self-antigens. Despite use of currently available therapies, patients experience relapses of their lupus. Over time, patients develop significant morbidity from the disease as well as from medications, including glucocorticoids, used for treatment. The main purpose of this study is to compare two ways of treating SLE: 1) high-dose immunosuppressive therapy (HDIT) followed by HSCT and 2) currently available immunosuppressive/immunomodulatory therapies.

1. One group of study participants will undergo autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. With this treatment, they will first undergo mobilization, a process that removes hematopoietic stem cells from their blood. Then they will receive high doses of chemotherapy to suppress their abnormal immune systems, followed by the reintroduction of the purified stem cells to re-establish their immune systems.

   Medications are used to mobilize (i.e., encourage) blood cell precursors to multiply and move from the bone marrow to the bloodstream. These precursors (or autologous stem cells) can be harvested (collected) from the bloodstream during a process called apheresis and then transplanted (infused) back into the patient's body after chemotherapy has been given. HDIT can suppress the immune system, reducing the effectiveness or perhaps eliminating most of the immune cells that cause the progression of SLE. Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) following HDIT hastens the return of the body's ability to produce blood cells. HDIT with HSCT has been identified as a potential treatment alternative to standard chemotherapy treatments.

   One group of study participants will undergo autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. With this treatment, they will first undergo mobilization, a process that removes hematopoietic stem cells from their blood. Then they will receive high doses of chemotherapy to suppress their abnormal immune systems, followed by the reintroduction of the purified stem cells to re-establish their immune systems.

   Medications are used to mobilize (i.e., encourage) blood cell precursors to multiply and move from the bone marrow to the bloodstream. These precursors (or autologous stem cells) can be harvested (collected) from the bloodstream during a process called apheresis and then transplanted (infused) back into the patient's body after chemotherapy has been given. HDIT can suppress the immune system, reducing the effectiveness or perhaps eliminating most of the immune cells that cause the progression of SLE. Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) following HDIT hastens the return of the body's ability to produce blood cells. HDIT with HSCT has been identified as a potential treatment alternative to standard chemotherapy treatments.

   Participants assigned to the first treatment group will undergo mobilization with CTX and granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) beginning 2 weeks after randomization. In preparation for the transplant process. a central venous line (plastic tube) will be inserted into the neck or chest vein; this tube will be used to administer stem cells and medications and for drawing blood. IV CTX, followed by G-CSF, will be given injected under the skin beginning 3 days after CTX. G-CSF will be given for about 4 to 7 days, to boost the body's production of blood precursor cells. These precursor cells will be collected through the central venous line through apheresis. In this process, whole blood is collected through a needle in an arm vein and directed to a cell-separating machine, where the white cells are separated and saved. The rest of the blood is returned to the patient through the same needle. Several apheresis procedures will be required to collect enough cells for the autologous transplant.

   Within 3 weeks of the apheresis stem cell collection, the first group's participants will be admitted to the hospital and will undergo a five-day conditioning regimen consisting of IV CTX and rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin (rATG). This regimen will suppress the malfunctioning immune system and prepare the patient's body to receive the precursor cells previously collected during apheresis. The stem cells will be infused after the five-day conditioning regimen. The return of the precursor cells is called autologous stem cell transplantation. During the hospitalization a specialized team of transplant physicians and nurses will closely monitor the participants until their bone marrow recovers and the participants are well enough to be discharged. The hospital stay will be approximately 21 days after the autologous stem cell transplant. Upon discharge, the patient will return home and will follow-up at the treatment center at Weeks 1 and 3 post-transplantation for close monitoring by the transplant team. Participants will also be followed by the study rheumatologist monthly at the treatment center for 30 months.

There will be an extension period for those patients that have completed their treatment and follow-up visits during the study's 5-year duration. Patients eligible for this trial are HCC patients with preserved liver function previously treated with any first line therapy.

Secondary objectives comprise the assessment of overall survival (OS), progression free survival (PFS) at 10 weeks, objective response rate (ORR), time on treatment, treatment exposure (dose intensity/dose reductions), toxicity, and quality of life (QLQ-C30).

* Women of childbearing potential must have a negative serum pregnancy test result within 14 days prior to initiation of study treatment.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Pregnancy or breastfeeding, or intention of becoming pregnant during study treatment or within at least 4 months.

* Presence of encephalopathy in past 12 months.

* Baseline QTcF \> 500 ms.
* Major surgical procedure, other than for diagnosis, within 4 weeks prior to initiation of study treatment, or anticipation of need for a major surgical procedure during the study.

While previous experiments evaluating candidate graphic warnings have been informative, they have used psychological outcomes, such as attitudes or quit intentions, but not actual cessation behavior (e.g., quit attempts). Furthermore, they typically expose participants to warnings in controlled but artificial experimental settings for a short period of time, using much lower frequency and shorter duration of warning exposure than found in the real world. This study addresses these issues by evaluating the impact of warnings on quit attempts by randomly assigning smokers to have their cigarette packs labeled with either a graphic warning or a Surgeon General's warning for four weeks.

Main hypothesis: Smokers randomized to receive graphic warnings on their cigarette packs will be more likely to report a quit attempt in the 4 weeks of the study than smokers randomized to receive a Surgeon General's label on their cigarette packs.

Secondary hypothesis: Smokers randomized to receive graphic warnings on their cigarette packs will have higher quit intentions at 4 weeks than smokers randomized to receive a Surgeon General's label on their cigarette packs, controlling for baseline quit intentions.","detailedDescription":"The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) proposed 9 new graphic warnings for cigarette packs in June 2011 to comply with the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act. However, tobacco industry litigation has delayed implementation of graphic warnings. A court ruling that struck down the labels criticized FDA for failing to "present any data - much less the substantial evidence required under the federal law - showing that enacting their proposed graphic warnings will accomplish the agency's stated objective of reducing smoking rates." This study will address this critique head-on by rigorously testing the impact of the graphic warnings on quit attempts in a randomized control trial.

Recruitment: Smokers will first undergo screening online or call the study center to complete the screening questionnaire over the phone. Study staff will schedule eligible smokers for 5 in-person visits. For each of their first 4 visits, smokers will be asked to bring the number of cigarettes they expect to smoke in an 8 day period.

Informed Consent: Prior to consenting smokers, research staff will visually inspect photo identification of smokers who report or appear to be under age 27. At the beginning of the first appointment, study personnel will explain the consent form and ask the smoker to read the form. Once the participant has finished reading the form, the study personnel member will ask the participant if he or she has any questions. Then both parties will sign the consent form and the participant will receive a copy of the consent form.

Randomization: After smokers have consented to participating in the study, study personnel will randomly assign them to a condition. The investigators will determine the randomization order a priori. Smokers have an equal chance of being randomized to receive one of four graphic warnings or one of four Surgeon General's warnings. They will receive the same warning on their packs during the study.

Assessment: Participants will complete 6 computer-based surveys during the study. The first appointment will take around 60 minutes and each subsequent visit will take around 30-45 minutes to complete. At their first visit, they will complete a "baseline pre-test," after which study personnel will show participants one of their cigarette packs with the assigned warning. Participants will be allowed to examine the pack. They will then return the pack to the study personnel and complete a "baseline post-test." At the next 3 appointments, participants will complete only one survey and their packs will be labeled. At the final appointment, they will only complete a survey.

Detailed description of the intervention: While participants are taking the survey, research staff will apply study warning labels to participants' cigarette packs during the first 4 visits. Participants assigned to the graphic warning condition will receive one of four graphic warning labels that will be applied and cover the top half of the front and back of their cigarette packs. The text for the graphic warnings was selected from the 2009 Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act and the images were proposed by the FDA. Participants in the Surgeon General's warning condition will receive one of four Surgeon General's Warnings that will be placed on the side of their packs on top of the Surgeon General's warning printed by the manufacturer. This procedure for the control condition is intended to control for the effects of labeling. The investigators will instruct participants in both conditions to use cigarettes from these labeled packs while they are in the study. Each week they will bring in 8 days' of cigarettes (one extra day to provide a buffer in case of rescheduled appointments or smoking more than anticipated) for labeling. Additionally, they will bring in any unused labeled packs from the previous appointment. The investigators will assess how many cigarettes participants smoke from labeled (i.e., study) and unlabeled (i.e., non-study) packs to calculate intervention dose (% of cigarettes smoked from labeled packs). At the end of the study, participants will receive a list of cessation resources. For individuals identified as being at high risk for developing this disease, adopting healthy lifestyle behaviors is a powerful way to lower that risk. However, starting and maintaining these new habits can be challenging. This study aims to test a comprehensive support program designed to help high-risk individuals make and sustain these positive health behavior changes.

Purpose The main goal of this research is to see if a specially designed 12-week health promotion program can effectively help high-risk individuals improve their lifestyle (e.g., diet, exercise, smoking/alcohol use), increase their knowledge about colorectal cancer, and strengthen their confidence and motivation to stay healthy.

Study Groups Participants in this study will be randomly assigned (like flipping a coin) to one of two groups:

1. The Intervention Group: This group will take part in the 12-week health promotion program.
2. The Control Group: This group will receive general health information or standard care but will not participate in the special program.

Procedures The program for the Intervention Group includes:

* Educational Workshops: Five in-person group sessions to learn about cancer prevention, create personal health plans, and solve problems with others.
* Online Support: Regular health articles and tips sent through a private WeChat group.
* Daily Check-ins: Using the WeChat group for simple daily check-ins on exercise, fruit/vegetable intake, and smoking/alcohol use to build habit.
* Peer Support: Being paired with a "health buddy" and interacting with other participants for motivation.

All participants will be asked to complete several questionnaires at the beginning of the study, during the program, and after it ends (at 3 months) to measure their knowledge, beliefs, and lifestyle habits.

Duration The active program lasts for 12 weeks.

Potential Benefits Participants in the Intervention Group may benefit from improved health habits, a better understanding of how to reduce their cancer risk, and increased social support. Participants in the control group will receive general health information. Risk Group 1, Women ages 25 - 80:

* The subject has tested positive for a deleterious germ line mutation in BRCA1 or BRCA2.

Risk Group 2, Women ages 35 - 80, Pedigree conditions can be satisfied by multiple primary cancers in the same person:

* The subject has a personal history of breast cancer diagnosed before or at age 50.
* OR the subject has a personal history of bilateral breast cancer
* OR the subject has one first-degree relative with breast cancer diagnosed before or at age 50.
* OR the subject has two breast cancers in the first or second degree relatives, same lineage, with at least one breast cancer diagnosed before or at age 50.
* OR the subject has three or more first or second degree relatives, same lineage, with breast cancer diagnosed at any age.
* OR The family contains at least one ovarian cancer diagnosed at any age in the first or second degree relatives.
* OR the subject is of Ashkenazi ancestry and has had breast cancer diagnosed at any age.
* OR The subject is of Ashkenazi Jewish ethnicity and has one first or second degree relative with breast cancer diagnosed at any age (must be in the same lineage as the Ashkenazi ancestry)
* OR The subject has a male relative with breast cancer diagnosed at any age
* OR The subject has a personal history of a positive genetic test result for a deleterious germline mutation in the P53 gene.
* OR The subject has tested positive for a deleterious germline mutation in one of the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes associated with the Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer Syndrome (HNPCC, also known as Lynch Syndrome) The MMR genes include MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2.
* OR the subject has a first or second degree relative with an identified deleterious germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation, but has not yet undergone testing herself.
* OR the subject has a first or second degree relative with an identified deleterious germline MMR gene mutation, but has not yet undergone testing herself.
* OR Probability of carrying a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation given family pedigree of breast and ovarian cancers exceeds 20% by any existing BRCA mutational probability model.

Risk Group 3, Women ages 45 - 80:

* Have measurement of CA125, HE4, MMP7 or Mesothelin exceeding the 95th percentile;
* OR have a relative risk of at least 2 based on the EpiRisk logistic regression model including age, family history, and other risk factors.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Removal of both ovaries for any reason.
* History of ovarian, fallopian tube cancer or peritoneal carcinomatosis.
* Currently pregnant.
* Unable or unwilling to provide informed consent.
* Unwilling to provide the name of a physician.
* Unwilling to sign informed consent and/or medical records release form.
* Current untreated malignancy (other than non-melanoma skin cancer).
* Currently receiving adjuvant chemotherapy or radiation therapy for cancer (except tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors +/- lupron). Patients who are being treated may enroll 3 months after completion of last treatment.
* Intraperitoneal surgery within the last 3 months (laparoscopy or laparotomy).
* A medical condition that would place subject at risk as a result of the blood donation, including but not limited to bleeding disorders, chronic infectious disease, emphysema or serious anemia.
* Subject has a family member who is a carrier of a BRCA or MMR gene mutation and the subject has undergone genetic testing that included the family mutation and no mutation was found, and there are no cases of ovarian cancer in the family.","healthyVolunteers":false,"sex":"FEMALE","minimumAge":"25 Years","maximumAge":"80 Years","stdAges":["ADULT","OLDER_ADULT"]},"contactsLocationsModule":{"overallOfficials":[{"name":"Nicole Urban, ScD","affiliation":"Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center","role":"PRINCIPAL_INVESTIGATOR"},{"name":"Beth Karlan, MD","affiliation":"Cedars-Sinai Medical Center","role":"PRINCIPAL_INVESTIGATOR"}],"locations":[{"facility":"City of Hope","city":"Duarte","state":"California","zip":"91010","country":"United States","geoPoint":{"lat":34.13945,"lon":-117.97729}},{"facility":"Cedars-Sinai Medical Center","city":"Los Angeles","state":"California","zip":"90048","country":"United States","geoPoint":{"lat":34.05223,"lon":-118.24368}},{"facility":"Stanford University","city":"Stanford","state":"California","zip":"94305","country":"United States","geoPoint":{"lat":37.42411,"lon":-122.16608}},{"facility":"Fox Chase Cancer Center","city":"Philadelphia","state":"Pennsylvania","zip":"19111-2497","country":"United States","geoPoint":{"lat":39.95238,"lon":-75.16362}},{"facility":"Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center","city":"Seattle","state":"Washington","zip":"98109","country":"United States","geoPoint":{"lat":47.60621,"lon":-122.33207}}]},"referencesModule":{"references":[{"pmid":"19945742","type":"BACKGROUND","citation":"Andersen MR, Goff BA, Lowe KA, Scholler N, Bergan L, Drescher CW, Paley P, Urban N. Disease status will be reevaluated 28 days (±7 days) from the end of the last RT treatment fraction by a direct clinical examination. PET-CT or CT will be conducted 12 weeks (±7 days) from the end of RT treatment fraction. No other anticancer treatments will be allowed during the treatment period and throughout the follow-up period. Patients with recurrent disease will be withdrawn from the study but followed-up for up to 60 months for survival.

A first interim analysis will be conducted 3 months after end of treatment to evaluate safety and response rate.

3 months after end of treatment"}]},"eligibilityModule":{"eligibilityCriteria":"Inclusion Criteria:

* Participant is eligible to be included in the study only if all the following criteria are met:

  1. The participant (or legally acceptable representative if applicable) provides written consent for the trial.
  2. Participant is at least 21 years of age on the day of signing informed consent
  3. Has a locally or centrally determined histologically or cytologically confirmed diagnosis of Epstein Barr Virus (EBV)-positive nasopharyngeal carcinoma Note: The EBV status is to be determined by the EBV-encoded small RNA in situ hybridization (EBER in situ hybridization \[ISH\]) assay. If EBV-positive status has been previously determined by EBER ISH assay, then no re-testing is required. If EBV status by EBER ISH assay has not been previously determined, tumour tissue from archival tissue may be submitted for EBV determination.
  4. Has recurrent or metastatic (R/M) disease not amenable to curative local therapy (surgery or radiation)
  5. Must have seen at least 1 prior line of systemic treatment and has progressed on prior platinum-based chemotherapy and anti-PD1 therapy in the R/M setting OR Progressed within 6 months of previous multimodal therapy containing platinum-based chemotherapy and anti-PD1 therapy in the locally advanced setting.
  6. Has measurable disease based on iRECIST.
  7. Has an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1.
  8. Has an adequate organ function as defined in the following table (table 1). Specimens must be collected within 10 days prior to the start of study treatment
  9. Willing to provide blood and tumour tissue samples (newly obtained biopsy if clinically feasible or archival specimen) to support exploratory biomarker analysis.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Participant is excluded from the study if ANY of the following criteria apply:

  1. Is currently participating in or has participated in a study of an investigational agent or has used an investigational device within 4 weeks prior to first dose of study treatment.
  2. Has prior anti-angiogenic therapy in the R/M setting or within 6 months as part of multimodality therapy in the locally advanced setting. \[Applies to cohort A only\]
  3. Has tumour that encases major arteries which in the opinion of the investigator carries high risk of vessel wall dehiscence.
  4. Has a condition requiring systemic steroid therapy (\> 10 mg daily prednisone equivalents) or any other form of immunosuppressive therapy within 14 days prior to the first dose of trial treatment.

     Note: Inhaled or topical steroids and adrenal replacement doses \<10 mg daily prednisone equivalents are permitted in the absence of active autoimmune disease. Patients are permitted to use topical, ocular, intra-articular, intranasal, and inhalational corticosteroids (with minimal systemic absorption). Physiologic replacement doses of systemic corticosteroids are permitted if \< or = 10 mg/day prednisone equivalents. A brief course of corticosteroids for prophylaxis (e.g., contrast dye allergy) or for treatment of non-autoimmune conditions (e.g., delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction caused by contact allergen) is permitted.
  5. Has active autoimmune disease that has required systemic treatment in the past 2 years (i.e. with use of disease modifying agents, corticosteroids or immunosuppressive drugs).

     Note: Replacement therapy (e.g. thyroxine, insulin, or physiologic corticosteroid replacement therapy for adrenal or pituitary insufficiency, etc) is not considered a form of systemic treatment.
  6. Has a history of (non-infectious) pneumonitis that required steroids or has current pneumonitis.
  7. Has hypersensitivity to ivonescimab or any of its components.
  8. Has a known additional malignancy that is progressing or has required active treatment within the past 3 years.

     Note: Participants with basal cell carcinoma of the skin, squamous cell carcinoma of the skin, transitional cell carcinoma of urothelial cancer, or carcinoma in situ (e.g. breast or cervical carcinoma in situ) that have undergone potentially curative therapy are not excluded.
  9. Has an active infection requiring systemic therapy, or serious non-healing wound, ulcer or bone fracture.
  10. Uncontrolled hypertension (failure of diastolic blood pressure to fall below 90 mmHg, despite the use of ≥ 3 anti-hypertensive drugs or systolic blood pressure greater than 150 mmHg).
  11. Recent cardiovascular thromboembolic event, such as the following:

      1. Cardiac chest pain, defined as moderate pain that limits instrumental activities of daily living, ≤ 4 weeks before enrolment
      2. Symptomatic pulmonary embolism ≤ 4 weeks before enrolment
      3. Any history of acute myocardial infarction ≤ 6 months before enrolment
      4. Any history of heart failure meeting New York Heart Association (NYHA) Classification III or IV (Appendix 4) ≤ 6 months before enrolment
      5. Any event of ventricular arrhythmia ≥ Grade 2 in severity ≤ 6 months before enrolment
      6. Any history of cerebrovascular accident ≤ 6 months before enrolment
  12. Persistent proteinuria of NCI-CTCAE Grade 3 or higher (\> 3.5 g/24 hours, measured by urine protein/creatinine ratio on a random urine sample).
  13. Clinically significant bleeding (NCI-CTCAE Grade 3 or higher) within 30 days prior to start of study medication.
  14. Has a history or current evidence of any condition, therapy, or laboratory abnormality that might confound the results of the trial, interfere with the subject's participation for the full duration of the trial, or is not in the best interest of the subject to participate, in the opinion of the treating investigator.
  15. Has known psychiatric or substance abuse disorders that would interfere with cooperation with the requirements of the trial.
  16. Is pregnant, breastfeeding or expecting to conceive or father children within the projected duration of the trial, starting with the screening visit through 120 days after the last dose of trial treatment.
  17. A woman of childbearing potential (WOCBP) who has a positive urine pregnancy test within 72 hours prior to randomization/allocation (see Appendix 3). If the urine test is positive or cannot be confirmed as negative, a serum pregnancy test will be required.

      Note: If 72 hours have elapsed between the screening pregnancy test and the first dose of study treatment, another pregnancy test (urine or serum) must be performed and must be negative for subject to start receiving study medication.
  18. Has a known history of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). Note: No HIV testing is required unless mandated by local health authority.
  19. Known active Hepatitis B (defined as hepatitis B viral load detected) or Hepatitis C virus (defined as HCV RNA \[qualitative\] detected) infection. Patients on anti-virals but with undetectable Hepatitis B or C viral loads are not excluded.

The incidence has risen by 497% since the late 1970's and is increasing worldwide due to continued mining and use of asbestos. For patients with mesothelioma who have relapsed after taking pemetrexed and cisplatin, there is currently no standard treatment, making this an urgent unmet need. Recent trials in this area have not found an effective treatment that improves overall survival.

Following a debate in the House of Lords, a national survey assessing the research priorities in mesothelioma found that 'exploiting the potential of immunotherapy' was a top priority. This trial was designed in response to that survey. It uses the immunotherapy agent nivolumab which blocks programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) receptor on activated T-cells (a type of white blood cell forming part of the immune system). Early research has found a dependency of mesothelioma on the PD-1 checkpoint. By attaching to PD-1, nivolumab blocks its action (checkpoint inhibition), preventing it from turning off the T-cell, and therefore allowing the immune system to work. PD-1 checkpoint inhibition has revolutionised the treatment of melanoma and it is hoped to be as effective in mesothelioma.

This trial is a randomised, double blind placebo controlled trial of patients with mesothelioma who are second or third relapse following a platinum based chemotherapy treatment.","detailedDescription":"Effective therapy for relapsed mesothelioma is an unmet need. Despite a significant number of clinical studies in the second line setting, no randomised study to date has been positive. The James Lind Alliance Priority Setting Partnership funded by the NIHR has identified immunotherapy as the number one UK research priority. To date there have been no placebo controlled randomised trials for mesothelioma using PD-L1 or PD-1 checkpoint inhibition. Early promising signals of activity relating to both PD-L1 and PD-1 targeted treatment in mesothelioma implicate a dependency of mesothelioma on this immune checkpoint, and support the development of a randomised phase III trial to evaluate the efficacy of nivolumab. CONFIRM will be the first ever placebo controlled, randomised phase III trial of a PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitor.

PD-1 checkpoint inhibition has revolutionised the treatment of melanoma and is now standard of care in non-small cell lung cancer, squamous cell cancer head and neck and classical Hodgkin's lymphoma. It is being assessed rigorously in numerous other cancers making its evaluation in mesothelioma timely in CONFIRM.

This trial is a randomised, double blind placebo controlled trial of patients with mesothelioma who are second or third relapse following a platinum based chemotherapy treatment. Patients will be randomised in a 2:1 ratio (nivolumab: placebo).

336 patients will be recruited from 25 UK centres with the last patient having a minimum of 6 months follow up.
